headline: Wisconsin Gov.-elect Crowley ties legalization to Medicaid cuts
dek: David Crowley says legal cannabis revenue could help offset federal Medicaid cuts; incoming Assembly Speaker Greta Neubauer calls legalization a priority.
key_points: Wisconsin Gov.-elect David Crowley told CNN that legalizing marijuana is one way to raise revenue as the state absorbs federal Medicaid cuts.
Greta Neubauer, elected on 10 November as the next Assembly speaker, said Democrats hope to pass legalization in the coming year.
Leaders have not decided whether legalization goes into the state budget or moves as a standalone bill.
Crowley has put the revenue at $80 million to $170 million a year; a 2023 state Department of Revenue estimate was nearly $170 million.
body: Wisconsin's incoming governor has given cannabis legalization a specific job: helping the state cope with federal Medicaid cuts. Asked by CNN on Tuesday how Wisconsin would handle reductions enacted under the federal budget law Republicans call the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Gov.-elect David Crowley said the state needs new revenue and named marijuana legalization as an example, according to Marijuana Moment.

On the same day, the legislative leaders who will write any bill set out their timing. Rep. Greta Neubauer, whom Assembly Democrats elected on Tuesday as their next speaker, said legalization is a priority and that Democrats hope to pass it in the coming year. That turns a long-running campaign promise into a 2027 legislative item.

For eight years, outgoing Gov. Tony Evers put legalization in his budget proposals, and Republican legislative majorities removed it each time. A limited medical cannabis bill cleared one committee in the 2026 session but went no further, and neither a Democratic adult-use bill nor a bipartisan decriminalization bill advanced.

The 3 November election changed that arithmetic. Crowley beat Republican Tom Tiffany by eight points, and Democrats flipped both legislative chambers, giving the party its first full control of state government since 2010, according to Cannabis Business Times. As we reported on 6 November, Democratic leaders said immediately afterwards that they intended to legalize within one to two years.

Crowley's case is mostly about money leaving the state. He told CNN that Wisconsin is one of the very few Midwestern states without legal marijuana and is losing tens of millions of dollars to Illinois, Minnesota and Michigan. In an October debate he estimated that full legalization could bring in between $80 million and $170 million a year for health care, and he has also linked the revenue to free pre-kindergarten.

There are official figures behind the upper end of that range. A Department of Revenue fiscal estimate on a 2023 legalization bill projected nearly $170 million a year in tax revenue, and a legislative analysis estimated that Wisconsin residents spent more than $121 million on cannabis in Illinois in 2022, generating $36 million in Illinois tax revenue, according to Marijuana Moment.
> Crowley's pitch is not about cannabis at all: it is a budget argument, and budget arguments tend to win in a year of federal cuts.

For comparison, Iowa's Gov.-elect Rob Sand, as we reported on 12 November, has pitched a cannabis tax worth about $54 million in its first year. Wisconsin's own fiscal note points to a similar start. The 2023 estimate, built on Michigan and Illinois sales data, projected $24.6 million from a 15% wholesale excise tax, $19.1 million from a 10% retail tax and $9.5 million in state sales tax in year one, according to the Marijuana Herald's reading of the note. By MetaFlora's arithmetic that is about $53.2 million in the first year, rising to $166.7 million by year three. Crowley's $170 million is therefore a mature-market number, not a first-year one.

His argument rests on demand that already exists: Wisconsin buyers who cross into neighbouring legal markets and whose spending, and tax, could be pulled back home. Evers' 2023–25 budget bill took the same approach; as summarised by the Legislative Reference Bureau, it would have legalized possession for adults 21 and over and for people 18 and over with certain medical conditions, and sent marijuana excise revenue to a community reinvestment fund.

The open question is the vehicle. Neubauer told reporters Democrats are still working out where legalization fits. Sen. Dianne Hesselbein, elected by Senate Democrats as the next majority leader, said it is to be determined whether cannabis goes into the biennial state budget or is proposed as its own bill.

The choice matters for operators. A budget route ties legalization to a must-pass bill and to the revenue numbers Crowley is citing, but it also folds detailed licensing rules into a sprawling fiscal package. A standalone bill gives lawmakers more room to set the structure of the market, from licence numbers to social equity rules, but competes for floor time.

Crowley has also said he wants guardrails in any law, including protections for children and accurate product labelling. Kevin Caldwell of the Marijuana Policy Project told Cannabis Business Times he expects Democrats to act in 2027, compared the situation with Virginia, where a new Democratic trifecta passed a commercial adult-use law, and said he hopes medical patients get a carve-out such as exemption from an excise tax.

Polling gives the new majority cover. A Marquette Law School poll released last year found that two in three Wisconsin voters support legalizing marijuana. Neubauer said after the election that legalization is very popular and that Democrats intend to listen to voters, and she has said the party hopes to raise revenue from it, according to WKOW-TV.

The legislature convenes in January, when the new majorities take their seats and Neubauer is formally elected speaker. The first signal will be whether Crowley includes legalization in his first budget proposal, and with what revenue estimate. Watch also for a standalone bill from Democratic leaders, the structure they propose for licences, and whether a medical-only programme is offered as a first step or folded into a single adult-use law.
